The Period of the Rise of Islam

According to Qur’anic logic, the human being, born from earthly clay, is raised above the angels and the rest of creation. Everything in the heavens and on earth is even described as being placed at humanity’s service.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This special status may itself be one expression of the connection between the human world and the unity of the universe as a whole.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But this view of the human being immediately raises another question:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
If the human being holds such a high position, does this mean that he acts—or chooses not to act—through his own will?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Is he free from a compulsion that would cancel his own will?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
In other words, can he freely choose to act or not to act and therefore be responsible for what he does, whether good or evil?
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Or does Islam place this question under the broader principle that links the entire universe to one supreme will, the will of the one God, just as the universe is also linked by the unity of its existence through its single Creator?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This question would confront Muslims later as Arab-Islamic society developed.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It would become a major intellectual and ideological problem occupying Arab-Islamic thought throughout the Middle Ages.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
During the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, the problem began as a quiet dialogue between thought and social reality.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Under Umayyad rule, that dialogue increasingly became an open conflict between thought and political power.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Later still, the struggle over the same problem increasingly took place between one body of thought and another.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Its social and political roots almost disappeared behind the dust of the intellectual and philosophical struggle—first between the Muʿtazila and their opponents, and later between philosophy and its opponents.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
We will return to this problem in a later section of the book dealing specifically with divine decree.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
For now, what matters is its connection with the question of the human being as Islam presented it during the period of Muhammad’s mission.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The issue is the basic place Islam gave the human being within its unified vision of the world.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Within that framework, what position did Islam take on human freedom of will?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
And what follows from that freedom: is the human being responsible for every action and every form of behavior that comes from him?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The foundational texts—the Qur’an and the Sunna—do not give one absolute and unambiguous answer.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
On the surface, the relevant texts point in two different directions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Some appear to affirm that human beings are free to act or not to act.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Others appear to deny that freedom and to connect every human action to the will that is the source of every other will in the universe: the will of the one God.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

This question too therefore becomes connected to the central issue of the Islamic message: establishing monotheism as a religious belief, as a social framework replacing the tribal framework, and as the theoretical basis of the ideology of the social order that would emerge as Islam triumphed, spread, and built lasting institutions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Consider, for example, these Qur’anic verses:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it. (Surat al-Zalzala, verses 7–8)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Whoever does good does so for himself, and whoever does evil does so against himself. (Surat al-Jāthiya, verse 15, and Surat Fuṣṣilat, verse 46)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Whoever wishes may believe, and whoever wishes may disbelieve. (Surat al-Kahf, verse 29)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The first two passages plainly say that every person must bear responsibility for what they do, whether good or evil, small or great.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
And the logic of responsibility seems to require that human action be connected to freedom of action.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The third verse appears to strengthen this conclusion. On its surface, it leaves belief and unbelief to the choice of the person who believes or disbelieves.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But alongside verses like these, we find other Qur’anic passages whose apparent logic points in a different direction:
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Whoever God wishes to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wishes to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted, as though he were climbing into the sky. In this way God places defilement upon those who do not believe. (Surat al-Anʿām, verse 125)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
You do not will unless God wills. (Surat al-Dahr, verse 30)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Early Muslim scholars devoted enormous effort to this apparent conflict between Qur’anic verses.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
They tried to bring all the texts together under a single logic in which no contradiction remained.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

That great intellectual effort grew out of political conflicts that produced an increasingly active world of ideas. Different views, schools, and ideologies struggled with one another until the Muʿtazila gave these debates a more developed form of rational inquiry.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
From there, the debate moved more specifically into philosophy.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
And from this atmosphere of intellectual and ideological conflict emerged the philosophical movement whose highest expression was what we call Arab-Islamic philosophy.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
We can therefore see how a creative intellectual movement, in both its foundations and its later developments, arose and grew on the intellectual ground created by Islam.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

This is why, as we said earlier, the basic unity of Arab thought rests on the common ground from which this entire movement emerged, even though its different currents later came to disagree with one another in fundamental ways.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Islam was that common, unifying ground.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
C — The Development of Islamic Legislation
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The Islamic mission spent thirteen years in Mecca without achieving victory. One reason was that the commercial leadership of Quraysh, as a social group developing into a class, was unable to understand its own long-term class interests. It did not yet see that those interests would not ultimately conflict with the social order Islam would create once the Islamic faith had won.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

But those thirteen years were filled with an enormous struggle between two forces. One drew its strength from traditional authority and material power. The other drew its strength from an unshakable belief in the new message and an extraordinary ability to endure fierce persecution without giving way.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Those years prepared the founder of the new faith and his companions, and they prepared the movement itself, for the much greater struggles still to come. Islam would face many more battles before it could establish itself firmly enough to move in step with the course of human development for an entire historical stage.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The struggle between Mecca and Islam eventually had to take a new direction. After thirteen years, the conflict could no longer be settled within its old limits. The great migration to Medina opened the way to this new phase.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
How did that road open, and how did the new phase begin?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
To answer that, we first need to understand how Medina, the new destination of the migration, differed from Mecca at the time.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

As we have seen, Mecca was a barren town in a “valley without crops.” Yet it had grown into an important commercial center and a religious center. Its great merchants had turned its religious importance to the advantage of their own interests as the group that controlled the town’s material, social, and religious life.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Because of Mecca’s special circumstances, together with the wider historical conditions of the Arabian Peninsula that we discussed in the first chapter, this rapidly growing commercial center developed a distinctive class structure. Sharp contradictions emerged within it. These conditions were likely to create a setting in which a movement could arise in Mecca and address the whole peninsula, answering the historical need for a major transformation of pre-Islamic Arab society.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Islamic mission appeared in precisely this setting.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But it met resistance from the very social group that, historically, was destined to play a leading role in the coming change. That group had a distorted understanding of its own interests.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam

It was an agricultural town, and its people had long worked mainly in farming. It had no large agricultural estates. Nor did it enjoy Mecca’s commercial standing or the religious importance that had helped make Mecca a major trading center. Social divisions in Medina had therefore not developed enough to create the same sharp conflicts between different groups of the population.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Permanent agricultural settlement had also led to the growth of several villages around Medina. Most were inhabited by settled tribes. The most prominent were the Aws and the Khazraj.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Before them, Jewish tribes had already settled in the area. The three most important were Banū al-Naḍīr, Banū Qaynuqāʿ, and Banū Qurayẓa.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Medina’s Jews did not work only in agriculture. They were also active in trade and in metalworking and jewelry-making as skilled crafts. They also spread the practice of lending at very high interest among poorer groups, including agricultural workers and the poor of the local tribes.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
2 — The Struggle Between Mecca and Medina
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That was the general character of Medina at the time.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The great difference between Mecca, with its commercial and religious importance, and Medina, which was mainly agricultural, may have encouraged the Aws and Khazraj—the two leading tribes of the Medina region—to raise the standing of their own town by embracing the Islamic movement after years of persecution by Mecca’s commercial leadership.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Their leaders may have hoped that by supporting Islam, they could eventually transfer some of Mecca’s importance to Medina if Islam won through their help.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Was this ambition, and this hope, behind the bold decision of the two tribal leaderships to begin negotiating—secretly at first—with the early Muslims?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
There is little reason to rule this out. In fact, what happened after those negotiations fits this interpretation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

During the pilgrimage season of 621 CE, twelve men came to Mecca—ten from the Khazraj and two from the Aws. They brought Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh, the founder of the Islamic mission, their decision to pledge allegiance to him.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

He met them at al-ʿAqaba, a pass between Mecca and Minā. The meeting ended with what became known as the Pledge of al-ʿAqaba. This pledge was an extremely important practical step in opening the historic road of migration to Medina.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
A year later, in 622 CE, the migration began.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
News had reached Mecca that the pledge had found fertile ground in Medina: conditions there were favorable for accepting Islam, protecting it, and working for its victory.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The first Muslim emigrants numbered around one hundred. They slipped out of Mecca separately and in small groups. When they reached Medina, they found safety, and the people who had made the pledge fulfilled their promises completely.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Once the migration was completed with the arrival of Muhammad and his companions in Medina, the nature of the conflict changed greatly.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It was no longer only a struggle between Muhammad and his followers on one side and the commercial leadership of Quraysh on the other. It also became a struggle between Mecca and Medina.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Yet the heart of the conflict remained the same. The Islamic movement still corresponded to the historical need to transform the foundations of pre-Islamic Arab society. At the same time, that transformation was moving in a direction that would ultimately serve the development of the very social forces that had originally placed themselves in direct opposition to Islam.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Islam’s migration to Medina was therefore a decisive historical event. It changed both the future of this struggle and the future of the larger historical project that Islam was then called upon to carry out.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The first reason the migration mattered was that Islam had now found security and stability in Medina, away from the persecution it had faced in Mecca. It could therefore begin working out the details of the new social relationships within which it would operate.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The second reason was the positive support Islam received from the Anṣār, the people of Medina who supported the emigrants. Their support shifted the balance of power decisively toward Islam in its struggle with Mecca’s commercial aristocracy.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
After the migration, fierce military battles followed between the Anṣār and the Muhājirūn, the emigrants from Mecca, on one side, and the leaders of Quraysh who opposed Islam on the other.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The first side won repeatedly, while the second suffered repeated defeats.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Eventually the Meccan side gave in and invited the Muslims to negotiate the entry of the Islamic “army” into Mecca without a battle. In modern military language, Mecca was effectively treated as an open city to the Muslim army—and therefore to the Islamic movement itself, with everything that movement represented both as a religion and as a social order.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This happened in 630 CE, eight years after the migration.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Mecca therefore regained its privileged position. More than that, from the time of the “conquest” onward, it became a center of worldwide attraction.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Because the great migration was such a decisive historical event, it allowed Islam to move from a stage centered mainly on calling people to faith into a new stage in which the movement also taught and organized society through a system of law.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Islam was no longer only a faith. It was also becoming a body of law.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This meant taking on the task of organizing a society that was moving beyond its tribal structure and entering a new system of social relations, more developed than those of the pre-Islamic period.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This was the beginning of the legislative stage in Islamic history.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The legislation itself developed in stages.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
At first it was simple and temporary because it dealt with a simple and temporary social situation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Later, Islamic legislation became more complex, broader in scope, and more permanent.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
We can therefore distinguish between two types of legislation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The first practical legislation made immediately necessary by the migration dealt with the emergency problems of housing and daily life faced by the Meccans who had been forced to leave their homes and families as part of the Islamic migration.
